(MSVC, Microsoft's C++ compiler, gives volatile acquire/release semantics by default on x86 targets; that is a compiler extension, not the language.)

courseTitle: Memory reclamation: epochs, hazard pointers, RCU
lessonTitle: Choosing a scheme: read cost versus bounded garbage
md: Do not benchmark a reclamation scheme with one thread on an idle machine. The cost differences that matter, garbage growth under preemption and fence cost on long traversals, only appear with oversubscribed threads (more runnable threads than cores, so some are always preempted), update-heavy workloads and long data structures.

courseTitle: Memory safety bugs: overflows, use-after-free and friends
lessonTitle: Integer overflow and signedness: when the size math lies
md: Every allocation size and every length passed to memcpy should come from a computation that cannot overflow and a value that cannot be negative. When a size comes from a file or a packet, validate it against the real data first.

courseTitle: Metric learning and re-identification
lessonTitle: Batch hard: mining the hardest pairs inside a P x K batch
md: Batch hard needs K of at least 2, or there is no positive to take a max over. And because it always picks the extreme pair, label noise and outlier crops dominate the loss: Hermans and colleagues show such outliers in Market-1501 and MARS (a video-based re-ID dataset) in their supplementary material.

courseTitle: Microbenchmarking pitfalls: when the number lies
lessonTitle: Noise, repetitions and when a difference is real
md: Repeat, interleave, and report the mean with a confidence interval (or a median with its spread). Never decide from one run or from the best of N.

courseTitle: Miles: production RL post-training forked from slime
lessonTitle: Token-in-token-out: train on the tokens you actually sampled
md: `role_content_only` is marked high risk. A tool-calling turn often has empty visible text, so two turns that called different tools can match. The stored prefix then wins, and the trainer keeps a history showing a call the agent never made, silently.

courseTitle: Miles: production RL post-training forked from slime
lessonTitle: LoRA RL and the multi-LoRA training service
md: In LoRA RL the adapter is what moves: about 1 to 2% of the bytes for a rank-32 all-linear adapter, synced by IPC or NCCL broadcast with no merge. Multi-LoRA extends that to many tenants, with client-owned loops, packed cross-tenant passes and immutable adapter versions for sampling.

courseTitle: Mobile app security testing: OWASP MASVS and MASTG
lessonTitle: The attacker holds the phone: OWASP MAS and its threat model
md: Misconception: "no root detection" is automatically a finding. MASVS states that the absence of resilience measures "does not in itself constitute a vulnerability". It matters only when the profile includes MAS-R, for example to protect against fraud or cheating.

courseTitle: Mobile app security testing: OWASP MASVS and MASTG
lessonTitle: Local authentication: a fingerprint must unlock a key, not a boolean
md: Misconception: "we use Face ID, so the data is protected by Face ID." Only if the data is encrypted under a key that requires it. If the token sits in UserDefaults or SharedPreferences, the prompt protects nothing from someone with the device's files (lesson 4) or a hook (lesson 5).

courseTitle: Multi-head latent attention (MLA)
lessonTitle: Build an MLA layer and prove the two forms agree
md: Checklist when porting MLA: normalize the latent only, and cache the normalized latent; rotate only $q^R$ and $k^R$, with the same pair layout as the checkpoint (interleaved here); scale scores by $1/\sqrt{d_h + d_h^R}$, times the YaRN factor for long-context checkpoints; and compare against the plain form before trusting any speedup.

courseTitle: Serving many LoRA adapters on one base model
lessonTitle: Batching different adapters: Punica's SGMV kernel
md: SGMV groups rows by adapter and runs all segments in one launch, so a batch can mix adapters while the base matmul stays shared. Its cost grows with the number of distinct adapters and their rank, because each one's weights must be read.

courseTitle: Multi-query retrieval: many phrasings, one fused result
lessonTitle: Drift, redundancy, reranker budgets, and when to skip it
md: Use multi-query when recall is the bottleneck because users word things differently from the corpus, and the next stage can absorb more candidates. Skip it for precise lookups, compound questions (decompose instead), tight latency budgets, and pipelines where a fixed reranker budget already decides the outcome. Measure end-to-end, not just first-stage recall.

courseTitle: Multi-token prediction: training GPTs to look ahead
lessonTitle: Why lookahead helps, and where it does not
md: These are intuitions, not proofs. The paper itself titles this section 'Why does it work? Some speculation'. Treat them as reasons MTP could help, then check the experiments.

courseTitle: Muon, Shampoo and SOAP: optimizers that treat weights as matrices
lessonTitle: Muon: orthogonalize the momentum with a few matrix multiplies
md: Muon does not produce an exactly orthogonal matrix. The reference implementation's docstring says the result is closer to $US'V^\top$ with the entries of $S'$ roughly uniform in $[0.5, 1.5]$, and that this does not hurt model performance. The Moonlight team also found 10 steps gave a more accurate result than 5 but no better training.

courseTitle: muP: tune a small model, transfer hyperparameters to a large one
lessonTitle: Why the best learning rate drifts as models get wider
md: muTransfer has three steps: parametrize the target in muP, tune a smaller version of it, copy the tuned HPs to the target. It works because muP makes the optimal HPs converge to fixed values as width grows.

courseTitle: muP: tune a small model, transfer hyperparameters to a large one
lessonTitle: muTransfer in practice: what transfers and what it saved
md: Don't expect dropout or weight decay tuned on a small proxy to be optimal for a much larger model trained on different amounts of data. The paper also notes that muTransfer may not be enough for fine-tuning on small datasets, where regularization matters most.

courseTitle: Mutexes, spinlocks and futexes: how locks really wait
lessonTitle: When spinning wastes the CPU, and how much to spin
md: `spin_loop()` is not `yield` (such as Rust's `std::thread::yield_now()`, which asks the operating system scheduler to run another thread for now). It is a hint to the CPU, not to the scheduler: a thread spinning with it still occupies the CPU for its whole time slice.

courseTitle: MVCC and transaction isolation levels
lessonTitle: Snapshots: how each transaction picks its version
md: Visibility is decided at read time by comparing tuple stamps against the reader's snapshot. Changing *when* the snapshot is taken changes what a transaction sees, without touching the data.

courseTitle: Named entity recognition: tagging spans in text
lessonTitle: The task: pull typed spans out of running text
md: An NER system is three pieces that must agree with each other: a **tag set** that can represent any set of non-overlapping spans, a **model** that scores tag sequences, and a **decoder** that turns tags back into spans. Most NER bugs live in the seams between them, not in the model.

courseTitle: Native sparse attention: NSA and DeepSeek Sparse Attention
lessonTitle: Picking blocks: importance scores come for free
md: Top-n selection itself is not differentiable, but NSA does not need it to be. The scores come from the compression branch, which is trained by the ordinary language modeling loss through its own output, and the selected tokens are trained through the selection branch's attention. No auxiliary loss is required.

courseTitle: Near-duplicate image search with perceptual hashes
lessonTitle: PDQ, learned copy detectors and building a real pipeline
md: Global hashes, PDQ included, do poorly when one image is a **crop** of another; the PDQ document lists deep crops as out of scope. ImageHash's documentation shows how fast aHash degrades with rotation on its test image: 2 bits at 1 degree, 11 at 6 degrees, 21 at 26 degrees. Large borders, overlaid text and memes also defeat them.

courseTitle: Network attacks and defences
lessonTitle: Where the attacker stands: on-path, off-path and on your LAN
md: Know the position before you pick the defence. Encryption (TLS) defeats on-path reading and rewriting of content. Unpredictable numbers (random ports, sequence numbers, IDs) defeat off-path guessing. Switch features such as MAC limiting, DHCP snooping and ARP inspection stop local attackers from becoming on-path.

courseTitle: Network attacks and defences
lessonTitle: Flooding DNS and HTTP/2: Dyn 2016 and Rapid Reset 2023
md: Application-layer floods win through asymmetry: a cheap action for the client (open and cancel a stream) that is expensive for the server. Defences measure behaviour per connection and close abusive connections outright, because per-request blocking leaves the cheap channel open. The pattern recurs: MadeYouReset (CVE-2025-8671, 2025) uses malformed control frames to make the server reset streams itself.

courseTitle: Network traffic analysis: Wireshark, Zeek and Suricata
lessonTitle: Zeek's protocol logs and pivoting with uid, fuid and Community ID
md: Two IDs carry most investigations: Zeek's uid joins logs about one connection, fuid joins logs about one file. Community ID extends the join to other tools. Learn to move between them quickly; it is most of the job.

courseTitle: Network traffic analysis: Wireshark, Zeek and Suricata
lessonTitle: Network forensics for incident response: a worked IcedID investigation
md: Capture and analyse only traffic you own or are authorised to monitor. Practice pcaps of real infections contain working malware and sometimes real personal data from the lab: open them on an isolated, non-Windows machine and never run extracted files.

courseTitle: How networks work, seen by an attacker and a defender
lessonTitle: Ports, sockets and NAT
md: NAT is not a firewall. It drops unsolicited inbound packets only as a side effect of having no table entry. Port-forwarding rules, devices that open forwards automatically, IPv6 (often no NAT at all) and connections started from inside all bypass that "protection". Use an actual firewall policy.

courseTitle: NUMA: placing memory and threads on multi-socket machines
lessonTitle: First touch: the thread that writes a page first picks its node
md: malloc chooses addresses, the first write chooses the node. Initialize data in parallel with the same pinned threads and the same partitioning that will later use it.

courseTitle: NVMe and SSD internals: FTL, garbage collection, write amplification
lessonTitle: Wear leveling, TRIM, hot and cold data, endurance
md: Lifetime and throughput both scale with 1/A. The levers to lower A are all about making victim blocks emptier: more spare, TRIM of dead data, writes that are large and sequential, and grouping data that will die at the same time.

courseTitle: Object detection and counting
lessonTitle: Training and tuning a detector in practice
md: The AP number picks the model; the confidence threshold, chosen on validation data that looks like deployment, decides how it behaves.

courseTitle: Observability: metrics, traces, dashboards and SLOs
lessonTitle: What metrics, traces and logs can each answer
md: The shape of the data decides which questions you can ask. Metrics answer "how often, how slow, for everyone". Traces answer "where did the time go inside this one request". Logs answer "what exactly happened at this instant".

courseTitle: Observability: metrics, traces, dashboards and SLOs
lessonTitle: SLOs, error budgets, burn-rate alerts, and the 03:00 dashboard
md: A dashboard is an ordered list of questions, not a list of metrics. Start with the SLO burn rate (are users hurt), then symptoms (what is broken), then causes and changes (why), then one link into a single trace (prove it).

courseTitle: OCR and document understanding: from pixels to fields
lessonTitle: Judging answers on documents with ANLS
md: ANLS = average over questions of the best (1 minus normalized edit distance) against any ground truth, zeroed when the distance reaches 0.5. It rewards nearly right reading, not semantic equivalence.

courseTitle: OS security, privilege and isolation
lessonTitle: Privilege separation: OpenSSH's design case
md: Privilege separation protects only the code that was moved into the unprivileged half. regreSSHion (CVE-2024-6387, covered in linux-for-security) was a signal-handler race in sshd's privileged code which, in Qualys's words, "is not sandboxed and runs with full privileges". That is why OpenSSH keeps shrinking the privileged parts: the 9.8 and 10.0 splits move more code out of them.

courseTitle: OSINT: open-source intelligence, done ethically
lessonTitle: Ethics and law first: public is not the same as permitted
md: Ask legal, authorised, ethical before every task. Public data is still personal data; combining it can create a harm none of the pieces had alone.

courseTitle: OSINT: open-source intelligence, done ethically
lessonTitle: Verifying images and claims: provenance, reposts and hashes
md: Ask where and when an image first appeared before asking whether it was edited. Perceptual hashes find reposts; provenance and corroboration decide the claim.

courseTitle: OSINT: open-source intelligence, done ethically
lessonTitle: People-search sites, data brokers and protecting your own footprint
md: Understand the people-data industry so you can defend against it: brokers sell profiles, attackers use them, and you shrink exposure with settings, separation, MFA and removal requests.

courseTitle: Building large projects from source (CMake, CUDA builds)
lessonTitle: CUDA builds: PTX, cubins and the architecture list
md: Cubins run only on the same major CC with an equal or higher minor; PTX JIT compiles forward to any equal or higher CC. Ship cubins for the GPUs you target plus PTX for the newest one, and keep the list short for development builds, because every entry multiplies CUDA compile time.

courseTitle: CI pipelines and test suites: from red checks to reliable tests
lessonTitle: Diagnosing and fixing flaky tests: order, state and timing
md: Flaky means uncontrolled state. Reproduce with the exact node id, order seed and loop count, find the state, and control it with a fixture. Reruns and quarantine are temporary and cost real signal.

courseTitle: Code review: responding to and giving review
lessonTitle: Review by email: patch versions and trailer tags
md: Whatever the tool, the author's loop is the same: answer every comment, change the code where the reviewer was right, record what changed between versions, and carry earned review credit forward only while it still applies.

courseTitle: Git workflow for pull requests: fork, branch, rebase, sign-off
lessonTitle: Fork, clone and two remotes: origin and upstream
md: Misconception: "syncing my fork" updates my laptop. GitHub's Sync fork button updates the fork on GitHub; `git fetch upstream` plus a merge updates your local copy. GitHub's docs point out that syncing locally does not update the fork on GitHub until you push. They are separate repositories.

courseTitle: Git workflow for pull requests: fork, branch, rebase, sign-off
lessonTitle: Sign-off, the DCO, and how your commits land upstream
md: Misconception: `-s` signs the commit. It does not. `-s` (lowercase) adds a Signed-off-by text trailer, a legal statement. `-S` (uppercase, `--gpg-sign`) adds a cryptographic signature made with your private key, by default through GPG (GNU Privacy Guard), that GitHub can show as Verified. A project may require either, both, or neither.

courseTitle: Open source licenses, CLAs and the DCO
lessonTitle: Inbound licensing: inbound=outbound and contributor agreements
md: Outbound is what users get; inbound is what the project gets from you. Inbound=outbound needs no paperwork; a CLA is a one-time signed grant, often with an explicit patent license and a statement about your employer.

courseTitle: Performance PRs: benchmark evidence and regression checks
lessonTitle: Reporting honestly: geomeans, many benchmarks and costs
md: Do not cherry-pick. Quoting only the best benchmark, dropping a regressed one, or rerunning until a borderline result flips are all ways to make noise look like a win. Reviewers who rerun your commands will find out.

courseTitle: Reproducing bugs: minimal repros, delta debugging and git bisect
lessonTitle: What a maintainer needs: a failure they can run themselves
md: A screenshot of a traceback is not complete. The maintainer cannot search it, copy the line numbers, or paste it into a test. Stack Overflow's guide says plainly: do not use images of code; paste text.

courseTitle: Writing a reviewable pull request
lessonTitle: Why a reviewer sends a big pull request back
md: The right size for a PR is **one self-contained change**: it does one thing, includes its tests, and leaves the system working. Line counts are a symptom; focus is the goal.

courseTitle: PagedAttention and prefix caching
lessonTitle: Why contiguous KV allocation wastes most of the memory
md: Knowing the exact output length would not fix this. Orca (Oracle) assumes perfect knowledge and still stores real token states in only 38.2% of KV memory, because contiguous chunks of different sizes still fragment the space and still cannot be shared.

courseTitle: Penetration testing methodology and recon
lessonTitle: What a penetration test is, and what it is not
md: A scan asks *what might be wrong*. A pentest asks *what can an attacker actually do here, inside this scope*. A red team asks *would we notice and stop them*. A bug bounty asks the crowd, continuously, within published rules.

courseTitle: Penetration testing methodology and recon
lessonTitle: Attack surface management: recon as a defender
md: Attackers run recon against you continuously and for free. Run it yourself first: inventory what is exposed, diff it on a schedule, and treat every unexpected change as an incident until explained.

courseTitle: perf and flame graphs
lessonTitle: A profiling workflow, its costs and its blind spots
md: Comparing two flame graphs by eye is error-prone because widths are relative to each graph's own total. To check a fix, record both under the same load and diff the folded files (a differential flame graph), and make sure you have enough samples for the change to stand out from noise.

courseTitle: Phishing, social engineering and email security
lessonTitle: Why people are the most attacked surface
md: Common misconception: "only careless people fall for phishing". The UK NCSC (National Cyber Security Centre) notes that people click for many reasons, including situational ones such as being busy and stressed, and that blaming them does not work. Blame also stops people reporting mistakes, which is the signal defenders need most.

courseTitle: Phishing, social engineering and email security
lessonTitle: Business email compromise and invoice fraud
md: BEC defeats technical email security by design: the best version comes from a real, authenticated account. The control that stops it is a payment process that does not trust email for changes to where money goes.

courseTitle: Pointers, memory layout, struct padding and alignment
lessonTitle: Layout for the cache: arrays of structs versus structs of arrays
md: Lay data out the way your hottest loop reads it: fields used together in the same line, fields read alone in their own array, rarely used fields out of the way, and data written by different threads on different lines.

courseTitle: Post-quantum cryptography and migration
lessonTitle: Grover's algorithm, and why AES-128 is still fine
md: NIST's verdict in IR 8547: symmetric primitives with at least 128 bits of classical security meet **security category 1** (the lowest of NIST's five post-quantum levels, listed next), and NIST does not expect to transition away from them. Only the few 112-bit ones are disallowed in 2030. Spend the migration budget on RSA and elliptic curves, not on re-keying AES-128.

courseTitle: Post-quantum cryptography and migration
lessonTitle: Deadlines and a migration plan you can defend
md: Dates differ by regulator, but the order of work does not: inventory, then key establishment on anything recorded today, then signatures, PKI and devices, all finished by 2035. The NIST dates apply at every key size; a 4096-bit RSA key is deprecated after 2030 like a 2048-bit one.

courseTitle: Prefetching, memory bandwidth versus latency
lessonTitle: Latency versus bandwidth: two different walls
md: Common misconception: "faster RAM will speed up my tree or hash-chain lookups." Faster transfer rates raise peak bandwidth, but a dependent chain of misses uses a tiny fraction of it. Its cost is set by latency, which has improved far more slowly.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: Pseudonyms and hashes are not anonymity: AOL 2006
md: Pseudonyms protect the name, not the person. They link all of one person's records, and those records (queries, routes, purchases) can identify them by content. Ask what a released record says, not only what field was deleted.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: Differential privacy: a promise about one person
md: Differential privacy is a property of the mechanism: on any two datasets differing in one person, every output is at most e^epsilon times likelier on one than the other. It survives post-processing and any auxiliary data, and epsilons add up across releases.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: Designing for less: data minimisation and purpose limitation
md: Minimise by architecture: collect less, coarsen at the edge, compute on the device, separate identity from content, enforce purposes in the access layer and in database grants, and default to the least sharing.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: Rights in code: access and erasure across every copy
md: Rights are requirements on every copy: build a data map (system, lookup key, export method, erase method), meet the one-month clock (Art. 12(3)), put backups beyond use, notify recipients, and verify identity in proportion to what you would hand over.

courseTitle: Privilege escalation and lateral movement
lessonTitle: Defending the path: segmentation, admin hygiene, EDR, HSE timeline
md: Escalation and lateral movement are a chain of small, valid-looking steps. Make each step harder (least privilege, unique and protected credentials, segmentation, patching known-exploited bugs) and make each step visible (forwarded logs, EDR, the event chains in this course), then make sure every alert has an owner.

courseTitle: Process reward models: grading reasoning one step at a time
lessonTitle: Using a PRM: reranking, step-level search and RL
md: Same scores, three uses: rerank finished solutions (weighted voting is a strong default), prune partial solutions in beam search (best on harder problems at modest budgets), or provide step-level rewards so RL can credit each step separately.

courseTitle: Processes, threads and the real cost of a context switch
lessonTitle: Who runs next: run queues, CFS, EEVDF and nice
md: Misconception: "nice 19 means it only runs when the machine is idle." A nice 19 task still has weight 15, so against one nice 0 task it gets about 1.4 percent. For truly leftover CPU, use the `SCHED_IDLE` policy, which the CFS document describes as even weaker than nice 19.

courseTitle: Product quantization (PQ)
lessonTitle: IVFADC: inverted lists with residual codes
md: Raising code size cannot fix a too-small nprobe. The paper notes that increasing the code length is useless if w is not big enough, because neighbors outside the probed lists are never scored. Tune nprobe first, then code size.

courseTitle: Protein design with diffusion over residue frames
lessonTitle: Sequence design, then the self-consistency check
md: Any structural comparison in this field is after optimal superposition. A reported RMSD of 1.4 Angstrom always means 1.4 after Kabsch alignment; the unaligned number is meaningless because it depends on where the coordinates happen to be written down.

courseTitle: Python for security work: parsing, automating and calling APIs
lessonTitle: Regular expressions: counting failed logins per address
md: A per-address threshold is easy to evade. Mandiant saw UNC5537 log in mostly through commercial VPN (virtual private network) addresses, and stuffing tools can spread attempts so each address fails only once or twice. Also count failures per username, and treat any success after failures as more important than the failures themselves.

courseTitle: Python for security work: parsing, automating and calling APIs
lessonTitle: Testing your script so it does not fail silently
md: Test the awkward inputs and the failure paths, not just the happy path, and keep tests offline with fakes. A test suite is what lets you change a detection script without wondering what you broke.

courseTitle: Query rewriting and decomposition
lessonTitle: Interleave, step back, or fan out: IRCoT, Step-Back and multi-query
md: Pick the pattern by the question's shape: a vague or context-dependent question needs one **rewrite**; a chain of facts needs **sequential decomposition** (Self-Ask, IRCoT); an over-specific question benefits from a **step-back**; a question that could be phrased many ways benefits from **multi-query** fan-out.

courseTitle: Race conditions and business logic flaws
lessonTitle: Business logic flaws: when correct code does the wrong thing
md: A logic flaw is an assumption the server never checks. To find one, list what the design assumes about users (what they send, in what order, how fast, how many accounts) and ask which assumption would pay them to break.

courseTitle: Race conditions and business logic flaws
lessonTitle: Limit overrun: one coupon, one balance, many parallel requests
md: Claim-first works only because the Set lives in this one process. Run two Node processes, or two servers, or keep the state in a real database, and the check and the claim are separate network calls again. The durable fix puts the claim where the state is: a unique constraint or a conditional update in the database (lesson 9).

courseTitle: Race conditions and business logic flaws
lessonTitle: Hidden sub-states: Kettle's GitLab email race (CVE-2022-4037)
md: Every request is a sequence of steps, so every endpoint that edits shared state has sub-states. Decide each security-relevant value once, carry it with the work, and make the state change atomic, rather than writing a value early and reading it back later.

courseTitle: Raft and Paxos consensus
lessonTitle: Raft safety: the election restriction and the Figure 8 trap
md: A Raft leader commits by counting replicas **only** for entries from its own current term. Older entries become committed indirectly, when a later current-term entry after them commits. Entries keep their original term number forever, which is why this rule is needed.

courseTitle: Feature engineering for ranking
lessonTitle: Query-document features: BM25 per field, coverage, proximity
md: Per-field BM25 features are not BM25F. BM25F (the subject of Elasticsearch's `combined_fields` query) merges term frequencies across fields before saturating. Separate per-field features saturate each field on its own and let the model weigh them. Both are useful; they are different numbers.

courseTitle: Ranking metrics: precision@k, recall@k, NDCG, MRR
lessonTitle: Three runs, seven verdicts: when metrics disagree
md: Disagreement between metrics is information, not noise. If binary metrics and exponential nDCG disagree, your system is trading coverage of relevant documents against putting the very best one first. Report at least one metric of each kind and say which user you care about.

courseTitle: Ransomware: how the business works, and how to resist and recover
lessonTitle: Case: Kaseya VSA and REvil, July 2021: one tool, many victims
md: Any tool that can run code on many machines (RMM, patch management, EDR consoles, software deployment) is Tier 0. Keep it off the internet, behind MFA and a dedicated admin network, and watch it as closely as a domain controller. CISA's MSP guidance adds: MSP accounts out of admin groups, a dedicated VPN for MSP traffic, and the MSP's activity logged into the customer's own monitoring.

courseTitle: RDMA: kernel-bypass networking with verbs
lessonTitle: Two-sided SEND versus one-sided READ, WRITE and atomics
md: Polling the trailer only works if the NIC writes the message in increasing address order. FaRM notes that many NICs, including theirs, guarantee this for RDMA writes but not reads. It is a hardware property, not a verbs promise: registering memory with `IBV_ACCESS_RELAXED_ORDERING` explicitly gives up write-after-write ordering.

courseTitle: Real-time multiplayer networking: WebSockets and state sync
lessonTitle: Showing other players: interpolation and lag compensation
md: Interpolation is not prediction. It never invents a position: it only blends two snapshots the server really sent. The cost is that every remote entity is shown late by the buffer delay, which is why aiming needs lag compensation.

courseTitle: Recommender systems and cold start
lessonTitle: Cold start: content for new items, bandits for new users
md: Space2 was shown only 23 times in 2000, although it is mobile users' second choice (0.25). Optimism-based exploration stops exploring once an arm looks clearly worse than the leader; that is the point, but it means some items get little data. Freshness boosts or explicit exploration slots are common additions.

courseTitle: Relational operators: joins, aggregation and planning
lessonTitle: Three ways to join two tables
md: Nested loop: cost about outer x inner-scan, works for any condition, great with an inner index and few outer rows. Merge join: one pass over each sorted input, needs sorted inputs and an equality key. Hash join: one pass over each input, needs an equality key and memory for the build side.

courseTitle: Replication and quorums: N, R, W and what they really buy you
lessonTitle: Leaderless quorums: why R + W > N makes reads overlap writes
md: $R + W > N$ is a counting argument, nothing more: if the write really sits on W of the N designated replicas and the read really asks R of those same N, they share a replica. Lesson 4 shows how failures quietly break the "same N" part.

courseTitle: Reward hacking: when optimizing the score breaks the task
lessonTitle: KL regularization: a leash, not a cure
md: KL regularization and early stopping limit the *amount* of optimization, which keeps you on the rising side of the Goodhart curve. They cannot tell a good high-reward behavior from a bad one. Only a better reward, a conservative reward, or an outside check can do that.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Governance, risk and compliance: three jobs and who decides
md: Governance decides who decides. Risk management decides what is worth doing. Compliance proves to outsiders that you did what you are obliged to do. They overlap, but a company can be compliant and still badly governed, or well governed and still breached.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Security economics: how much to spend (the Gordon-Loeb model)
md: Gordon-Loeb's lessons for engineers: spend where a dollar reduces the most expected loss, not where the scariest weakness is; for the paper's broad families of breach functions the optimum is at most about 37 percent of expected loss; and making controls more effective beats making budgets bigger.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: One control, many frameworks: CIS Controls, HIPAA and the crosswalk
md: Do not run one programme per framework. Write each control once, build it to the strictest applicable requirement, map it to every framework it satisfies, and attach evidence that is collected automatically. Start from CIS IG1 if you have nothing; use the crosswalk to answer everyone else.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Cyber insurance: what it pays, what it asks, what it excludes
md: Insurance does not replace controls or accountability. Regulators still fine you, customers still leave, and a claim can fail if your application overstated your controls or the event falls under an exclusion. Treat the policy wording as a contract engineers should read: what counts as a covered event, which notice deadlines apply, which incident responders you must use.

courseTitle: RL post-training infrastructure at scale
lessonTitle: Colocated or disaggregated: where the engines live
md: Colocation trades memory and switch time for zero idle pools. Disaggregation trades network sync and staleness for overlap and freedom to size each pool. The long tail pushes large reasoning runs toward disaggregated, asynchronous designs.

courseTitle: RL post-training infrastructure at scale
lessonTitle: Multi-turn agentic rollouts: tools, servers and token-in, token-out
md: A common misconception is that storing the chat transcript is enough, because the trainer can tokenize it again. Tokenizing is not the inverse of sampling: the policy may have sampled a non-canonical split, and tool parsers edit messages. Train on the ids the engine returned.

courseTitle: Root cause analysis: from correlated alerts to the actual cause
lessonTitle: Trigger, proximate cause, contributing factors, action items
md: "The root cause" is usually a decision about where to stop asking, not a fact. The SRE book is careful here: systems are complex, and it is likely that multiple factors, each individually not the cause, are jointly causes. Its template says Root Causes, plural. Note that a cause chain pointing at a person is a sign you stopped one question early.

courseTitle: Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)
lessonTitle: When score fusion beats RRF
md: RRF trades information for robustness: it ignores how far apart scores are, so it cannot be fooled by scale, but it also cannot use a confident gap. With labels and comparable scores, a tuned convex combination usually wins; without them, RRF is the safe default.

courseTitle: Rust in the Linux kernel: safe abstractions over unsafe C
lessonTitle: Intrusive lists, work items and condition variables
md: Misconception: "`wait` returns only after `notify`, so an `if` is enough." The CondVar docs say a wait may also wake spuriously, and with `notify_all` another waiter may have consumed the result first. Re-check the condition in a `while` loop every time `wait` returns.

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: The scheduling cycle: select_cpu, enqueue, dispatch, run
md: Where a task finally runs is decided when it lands in a local DSQ, usually inside `ops.dispatch()` on the CPU that is asking for work. `select_cpu` is an optimization: matching the final CPU saves a bit of work, and picking an idle CPU wakes it up.

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: Keeping tasks in BPF: custody, dequeue and user-space policy
md: If you hold a task anywhere other than a terminal DSQ, implement `ops.dequeue()` and drop your reference there. The kernel will re-enqueue the task after any property change, so a stale entry means a task is queued twice.

courseTitle: Secrets and key management
lessonTitle: How secret scanners find keys: patterns, entropy, verification
md: A scanner finds only what looks like a secret. A custom token with no prefix, a password of ordinary words, or a key split across two lines passes silently. If you issue tokens yourself, copy GitHub's design: a unique prefix and a checksum make your secrets findable by every scanner and cheap to validate.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: What a secure code reviewer is looking for
md: Review the flow, not the line: find each source, follow it to each sink, and check the control (validation, encoding, authorization) at each step. Then ask what the code assumes and whether an attacker can make that assumption false.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: Regular expressions that hang: ReDoS and the Cloudflare outage
md: A backtracking regex is safe only if every string has few ways to match it. Nested quantifiers and adjacent .* make the number of ways explode, so a short input can take seconds. Rewrite, bound the input, or use a linear-time engine.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: Rust: FFI boundaries, release-mode overflow and panics
md: Rust review checklist beyond unsafe: arithmetic on input uses checked_* or try_from, not + or as; every FFI call has a SAFETY comment covering NUL termination, pointer lifetime, ownership and lengths; and no unwrap, expect or unchecked index on anything an attacker controls.

courseTitle: Secure network protocols: IPsec, WireGuard, SSH, RADIUS and friends
lessonTitle: IPsec traps: weak PSKs, aggressive mode, NULL and old algorithms
md: IKEv2 does not make a weak PSK safe. A client that connects to a rogue gateway (for example on hostile Wi-Fi with a spoofed address) completes IKE_SA_INIT with the rogue and sends its own AUTH to it. RFC 7296 states that dictionary attacks on user-chosen PSKs "are not prevented in this authentication method". Strong random PSKs, or certificates, are the fix.

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: Bell-LaPadula: no read up, no write down
md: Bell-LaPadula protects secrecy only. Writing up is allowed, so a low-level process may overwrite a TOP SECRET file it cannot read. Nothing in the model protects the integrity of data; that needs a different model, next lesson.

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: The trust algorithm: criteria, scores and context
md: A score hides which factor failed. If a control must always hold (a patched OS for admin consoles, phishing-resistant MFA for payroll), make it a criterion, not a weight that other good signals can outvote.

courseTitle: Security automation and AI-assisted security operations
lessonTitle: Idempotent steps: designing work that is safe to run twice
md: Derive the key from the event, let the database or the API enforce it atomically, and reuse the same key on every retry. Then duplicates from webhooks, queues and retries all collapse into one effect.

courseTitle: Security automation and AI-assisted security operations
lessonTitle: When not to automate, and a design review checklist
md: Automate what is reversible, small and precisely triggered; cap and approve what attackers can trigger; keep irreversible, wide-impact and judgement-heavy steps with people; and give language models advice to write, never authority to act.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: How a vulnerability becomes public: disclosure, CVE and NVD
md: Path of a vulnerability: found, reported, fixed, numbered (CVE via a CNA), published with a patch, enriched by NVD (CVSS, CWE, products), patched by users. Attackers can enter at any point; the gap between patch release and patch install is where most damage happens.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: Who does security work: the job families
md: Five families: offence, defence (SOC, detection, IR), AppSec, cloud security and GRC. They need the same foundations this track teaches: how systems work, how attacks work, and how to read, script and explain.

courseTitle: Security leadership: strategy, programmes and teams
lessonTitle: From gaps to a roadmap: strategy, sequencing and dependencies
md: A strategy is a diagnosis, a choice (including what you will not do) and coordinated actions. A roadmap places those actions by dependency and capacity, with an owner and a measurable outcome for each item. Re-plan it every quarter and show the board what is unfunded.

courseTitle: Security leadership: strategy, programmes and teams
lessonTitle: Hiring and keeping people: what predicts performance
md: Hire with work samples and structured, independently scored interviews; do not filter on years of experience or credentials the job does not need. Keep people with growth paths, sustainable on-call and time to learn.

courseTitle: Writing and influence for security work
lessonTitle: Plain, direct and first: sentences a busy reader acts on
md: Hedging is not the same as honesty. "May potentially" hides uncertainty instead of stating it. If you are unsure, say what you know, what you do not, and how sure you are (the incident lesson later in this course gives you the words). If you are sure, do not hedge to sound modest.

courseTitle: Self-play and self-improvement: how models learn from their own output
lessonTitle: Why a model can teach itself: improve, then distill
md: The search policy is a better policy than the network that guided it. Training the network to imitate it is **policy improvement by imitation**. No human labels are used, but new information does enter the loop: from look-ahead, and from the game rules that score every finished game.

courseTitle: Self-play and self-improvement: how models learn from their own output
lessonTitle: Using failures and training the judge: V-STaR, the gap, Meta-Rewarding
md: Training the judge on its own meta-judgments imports new biases. By iteration 2 the meta-judge preferred the judgment with the higher score 97.68% of the time, the judge's mean score rose from 4.1 to over 4.7 out of 5, and position bias grew. Scores bunched near the top, which made responses harder to tell apart. Lesson 6 flagged the same risk: a judge's blind spots become the policy's target.

courseTitle: Semantic caching and prompt compression
lessonTitle: Prompt compression: pruning tokens with a small language model
md: Compression has costs of its own. The compressor runs on the critical path of every request. The compressed text is hard for humans to read, which makes debugging and audits harder. Exact strings (code, JSON, numbers, IDs) can be damaged by token deletion. And question-aware compression produces a different context for every question, so that context can no longer be served from the provider's prefix cache.

courseTitle: Server-side attacks: SSRF, deserialization, XXE and file handling
lessonTitle: Log4Shell: how logging a string ran code
md: Only `log4j-core` 2.x is affected; applications with just `log4j-api` are not, and Log4j 1.x has no lookups (its separate JMSAppender issue is CVE-2021-4104). But Log4j is often a *transitive* dependency: a library you use pulls it in, so "we do not use Log4j" needs checking, not assuming.

courseTitle: SGLang: RadixAttention, cache-aware scheduling, compressed FSMs
lessonTitle: Scaling out: TP, DP, DP attention, EP and cache-aware routing
md: Cache locality and load balance pull against each other. Sending every request of a hot prefix to one worker maximizes hits and can overload that worker; the balance thresholds exist to break locality when queues diverge. The gateway's trees are approximate: they are inferred from routed text, not read from the workers, so they can be stale.

courseTitle: Shortest-path routing on road graphs
lessonTitle: Real engines: turn costs, live traffic and time-dependent travel
md: No technique wins on every axis. Look at query time, preprocessing time, memory, how quickly new traffic weights can be applied, and whether turns and other metrics are supported. A static fastest-route server and a live-traffic service often choose differently.

courseTitle: SIMD: AVX2, AVX-512, Arm Neon and SVE from the lanes up
lessonTitle: Writing a vector loop: intrinsics, reductions and tails
md: Every hand-written SIMD loop has a vector body, a horizontal reduction and a tail. A vector reduction adds in a different order than the scalar loop, so float results can change, which is why compilers need permission to reassociate.

courseTitle: Slab, bump/arena and buddy allocators
lessonTitle: Bump allocation: a bounds check and a pointer add
md: "Arena" means different things in different allocators. In this lesson it is a bump region freed all at once. In jemalloc (a general-purpose malloc used by FreeBSD and Firefox, among others) and in glibc malloc (the GNU C library's allocator, the default on most Linux systems) an *arena* is an independent general-purpose heap with its own locks, used so threads contend less; you still free objects one by one there.

courseTitle: slime: RL post-training with Megatron and SGLang
lessonTitle: Moving weights from Megatron into SGLang
md: The colocated code keeps a comment worth remembering: SGLang returns from the update request after enqueueing GPU copies, not after they finish. Reusing the same flattened IPC buffer for the next bucket right away could overwrite memory SGLang is still reading and corrupt weights, so slime allocates a fresh buffer per bucket.

courseTitle: slime: RL post-training with Megatron and SGLang
lessonTitle: Train-rollout mismatch in slime: TIS, IcePop, R3 and score centering
md: A falling `train_rollout_logprob_abs_diff` is not proof of better learning, and a rising `tis_clipfrac` is not fixed by widening the clip: under IcePop every clipped token is lost signal, and under TIS a wider band lets rare tokens dominate. The guide's protocol: hold data, seed and evaluation fixed, change one mechanism at a time, and read reward alongside the mismatch metrics and, when async, staleness.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: Enrichment: asset, identity and intel context, and where it lies
md: Enrichment answers "what is this thing?", not "is this bad?". Treat every enriched field as a claim with a source and an age, show unknowns explicitly, and never let a single reputation score close or escalate an alert by itself.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: Talking to users, owners and leaders during an investigation
md: Never let an attacker-controlled message decide who you trust. A chat message saying "I'm from IT, please approve the prompt" is exactly what the Lapsus$ actors sent, per the CSRB. The same rule applies inside the SOC: verify urgent requests to disable monitoring or grant access through a second channel.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: Designing help-desk verification that holds under pressure
md: Misconception: "on-camera verification solves help-desk fraud". It raises the bar, but synthetic video and stolen ID images are already used against identity checks (FinCEN, 2024). Pair it with an out-of-band confirmation for anything privileged, and keep the most powerful admin accounts out of help-desk reach entirely.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: The sparse autoencoder: a wide, sparse dictionary for activations
md: An SAE is dictionary learning with a neural network: an encoder that picks a few latents, a decoder whose columns are the dictionary directions, and a loss that trades reconstruction against sparsity.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: Measuring an SAE and steering a model with its features
md: Judge an SAE by sparsity (L0), reconstruction (FVU) and downstream loss together, then verify interpretations causally. Steering by clamping a latent equals adding $(c - f_i)$ times its decoder direction while keeping the SAE error.

courseTitle: Spatial interpolation: IDW, variograms and kriging
lessonTitle: The semivariogram: measuring how similarity decays with distance
md: An empirical variogram from a handful of points is very noisy, and the fitted range and nugget can swing a lot with the bin edges or the fitting weights. Look at the plot, try a second binning and treat the parameters as uncertain, not as measured truths.

courseTitle: Speculative decoding: draft fast, verify in one pass, lose nothing
lessonTitle: Draft, verify, keep: the loop with greedy decoding
md: A common bug: after a rejection, keeping the target's distributions for later positions. Those were computed with the rejected guess in the context, so they condition on a token that is no longer in the output. Only the distribution at the first rejected position is valid.

courseTitle: Speech-to-text: log-mel features, Whisper, CTC and WER
lessonTitle: Whisper: a transformer over 30-second spectrogram windows
md: Whisper is an audio-conditioned language model. The encoder turns 30 s of log-mel into 1500 vectors; the decoder generates the transcript token by token, with language, task and timestamps expressed as tokens in the same sequence.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: The stack: memory that frees itself when a function returns
md: Stack memory lives exactly as long as the function call that created it. Allocation and release are a pointer adjustment, which is why the size must be bounded and why anything that must outlive the call has to go somewhere else: the heap.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: TLB reach, huge pages and shootdowns
md: TLB reach = entries x page size. Working sets beyond it pay a page walk on most random accesses; huge pages raise reach by 512 times, and every unmap in a multithreaded process may interrupt other CPUs.

courseTitle: Steering vectors and activation engineering
lessonTitle: Lab: build, sweep and evaluate a steering vector on a small chat model
md: Three things bite first attempts. The chat template inserts a default system prompt ("You are Qwen...") when you give none. Qwen's tokenizer turns "(A" into a single token, so the answer letter is not a separate position: read activations at the "(A" token and score the "(A" and "(B" tokens. And the hook must cope with both output types of a decoder layer. Print the tokens of one full prompt before anything else.

courseTitle: Streaming sensor pipelines: event time, watermarks, online filters
lessonTitle: Windows, watermarks and allowed lateness, step by step
md: Watermark = the processor's estimate of how far event time has progressed. It decides when a window first fires; allowed lateness decides how long the window can still be corrected; anything beyond is dropped or side-output. Every choice trades latency for completeness.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: Causal masks, teacher forcing and cross-attention
md: A causal mask sets the scores of future positions to minus infinity before softmax, so with teacher forcing every target position trains in one pass without seeing its own answer. Cross-attention is the same function with queries from the decoder and keys and values from the encoder.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: Training recipe, quadratic cost and what changed since 2017
md: "Transformer" does not mean "GPT" (generative pre-trained transformer, OpenAI's line of decoder-only language models). The 2017 model is an encoder-decoder for translation. Decoder-only language models keep only its masked self-attention stack; encoder-only models keep only the unmasked encoder.

courseTitle: Build a GPT from scratch
lessonTitle: Next-token prediction: turning raw text into training examples
md: Training is **teacher forcing on every position in parallel**: the true previous tokens are always the context, and all $B \times T$ predictions are scored in one pass. Generation is the opposite, one token at a time feeding its own outputs back in.

courseTitle: Build a GPT from scratch
lessonTitle: Generating text: the sampling loop, temperature, top-k and top-p
md: The model never stores the text it generated anywhere except in `idx`. There is no hidden memory across calls: anything older than `block_size` tokens is simply cropped away and cannot influence the next prediction.

courseTitle: Calculus and gradients: from slopes to backpropagation
lessonTitle: Many inputs: partial derivatives and the gradient vector
md: The gradient points in the direction of **steepest ascent**, and its length is that steepest rate. So $-\nabla f$ is the direction of steepest descent, the direction every gradient-based **optimizer** (the algorithm that updates the parameters during training) starts from.

courseTitle: Calculus and gradients: from slopes to backpropagation
lessonTitle: Backpropagation: the chain rule run backward through a graph
md: Gradient checks can fail for honest reasons: at a kink (a sharp corner) such as ReLU at 0 (lesson 2) or a max with ties, the function is not differentiable and the two sides disagree. Check at random points away from kinks, and in double precision.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: files, scripts, pipes and ssh
lessonTitle: File descriptors: why the order of 2>&1 matters
md: Misconception: `2>&1` *links* stderr to stdout permanently. It does not. It is a one-time copy of fd 1 as it is at that moment. Any later change to fd 1 leaves fd 2 where it was.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: files, scripts, pipes and ssh
lessonTitle: Job control and signals: Ctrl-C, Ctrl-Z, background jobs and trap
md: Ctrl-C is SIGINT, Ctrl-Z is SIGTSTP, `kill` is SIGTERM, `kill -9` is SIGKILL, and a closed terminal is SIGHUP. In a script, route every way out, signals included, through one `trap ... EXIT` cleanup.

courseTitle: Embeddings and representation learning: from IDs to vectors
lessonTitle: Evaluating and visualizing an embedding space
md: A t-SNE plot shows neighbourhoods, not geometry. Do not conclude that one cluster is more varied than another, or that two clusters are closer than a third, from the picture. Check such claims with distances computed in the original space.

courseTitle: GPU and inference basics
lessonTitle: Prefill and decode: FLOPs and bytes per generated token
md: Doubling peak TFLOP/s does almost nothing for batch-1 decode. What helps is moving fewer bytes per token (smaller or quantized weights: quantizing stores each weight in fewer bits, so 8-bit weights halve the bytes) or using each byte for more tokens (batching, next lessons).

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: Bits, bytes and hex: how numbers are stored
md: Misconception: "signed overflow wraps in C too." The hardware adder wraps, but in C, overflowing a signed integer is [undefined behavior](https://en.cppreference.com/w/c/language/operator_arithmetic), and compilers optimize on the assumption that it never happens. Only unsigned arithmetic is guaranteed to wrap modulo $2^n$.

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: Why memory is slow and how caches hide it
md: Performance is often decided by memory access patterns, not instruction counts. Touch memory sequentially, reuse data while it is still in cache, and keep hot data small.

courseTitle: How LLMs are trained: pretraining, SFT, RLHF
lessonTitle: From web crawl to training tokens: the pretraining data pipeline
md: Raw crawl becomes training data through extraction, filtering, near-duplicate removal, PII and contamination handling, then packing. Each step was chosen by training small models on the result, and a run then moves through stages: main pretraining, context extension, annealing.

courseTitle: How LLMs are trained: pretraining, SFT, RLHF
lessonTitle: RL with PPO: maximize reward, stay close to the SFT model
md: RLHF does not maximize reward. It maximizes reward minus beta times the KL from the SFT model, and beta sets how far the model may move to chase the reward model.

courseTitle: Inverted indexes and TF-IDF: how keyword search works
lessonTitle: Ranking with vectors and cosine similarity
md: The vector space model scores a document by the cosine between its tf-idf vector and the query's. Engines compute it by streaming the query terms' postings into accumulators, so documents that share no query term cost nothing.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Multi-file C: headers, include guards, static, extern and make
md: Headers hold declarations (`extern` variables, prototypes) behind an include guard; exactly one .c file holds each definition; `static` keeps helpers private. A Makefile lists what each file depends on, and make rebuilds only what is older than its inputs.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Object lifetimes: automatic, static and malloc'd memory
md: Before you keep a pointer, ask how long the object behind it lives. Locals die when their function returns, malloc'd memory dies at free, and realloc can retire the old address at any call.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Undefined behavior, and the tools that catch it
md: Develop C with `-Wall -Wextra -g -fsanitize=address,undefined` on, and fix every warning. Most of the pointer and lifetime bugs from this course then fail loudly at the exact line instead of corrupting memory silently.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: Borrowing: many readers or one writer
md: Shared XOR mutable: any number of `&T`, or exactly one `&mut T`, never both at the same point in the program. A borrow is live from creation to last use.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: When the checker says no: clone, Rc and RefCell
md: Default to borrowing; move when the callee should keep the value; clone when copies are cheap or necessary; use `Rc`/`RefCell` only for data with genuinely shared ownership.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: A matrix is a function that moves every vector
md: $A\mathbf{x}$ is both a stack of dot products (one per row) and a weighted sum of columns. The columns of $A$ are the images of the basis vectors, so they fully describe the map.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: Tensors, batches and broadcasting: shapes in real code
md: Broadcasting checks sizes, never meaning. A loss computed from (3, 1) predictions and (3,) targets averages 9 differences instead of 3 and raises nothing. Assert shapes where arrays from different places meet: `assert pred.shape == y.shape`.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Many features: linear regression in matrix form and feature scaling
md: With many features, predictions are $\hat y = Xw$ and the MSE gradient is $\frac{2}{n}X^\top(Xw - y)$. Its minimum solves the normal equations $X^\top Xw = X^\top y$. Features on very different scales stretch the bowl, so gradient descent crawls; standardizing them rounds it out.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Validation and penalties: choosing lambda, L2 and L1
md: Choose capacity and penalty strength by **validation** error and keep the test set for one final check. L2 (weight decay) shrinks every weight a little each step; L1 pins weak weights at exactly zero and so selects features.

courseTitle: Neural networks and backpropagation
lessonTitle: Why a single linear layer cannot learn XOR
md: Misconception: a deeper network of linear layers is more expressive. It is not; it is exactly as expressive as one linear layer. Another one: universal approximation means any network will learn any function. It only guarantees that suitable weights exist.

courseTitle: Neural networks and backpropagation
lessonTitle: Gradients through depth: vanishing, exploding and unlucky seeds
md: Backprop computes the exact gradient of the loss at the current weights; it does not guarantee a good solution. The loss surface of a network is not **convex** (bowl-shaped, so that every valley is the lowest one), so the starting point matters. Lesson: always check the loss curve, and try more than one seed.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Beyond physical memory: page faults, swapping and replacement
md: Memory is a cache for pages, and a disk-backed miss costs about 100,000 memory accesses. A replacement policy tries to approximate OPT using the past: LRU in principle, the use bit and the clock algorithm in practice, preferring clean pages.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Persistence: how a hard disk spends its time
md: A random disk I/O is almost all positioning: seek plus half a rotation, milliseconds, against microseconds of transfer. Make requests large and sequential, and let the scheduler order them by position.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Probability by counting outcomes, and what conditioning does
md: Conditioning means restricting attention to the outcomes consistent with what you know, then renormalizing so they sum to 1. Almost every formula in this course is that one idea applied carefully.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Covariance, correlation and the multivariate Gaussian
md: Correlation is not causation. Ice cream sales and sunburns are correlated because sunny weather drives both: a **confounder**, a third variable that causes both. The Deep Learning textbook by Goodfellow, Bengio and Courville makes the same point about conditioning: P(from Germany | speaks German) is high, but teaching someone German does not change where they are from.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Power and sample size: planning an A/B test before running it
md: Power depends on the effect size you assume. Choose the smallest effect worth acting on before you see data, not the effect you hope for and not the effect a finished test happened to show.

courseTitle: Scaling laws: predicting loss from model size, data and compute
lessonTitle: Run your own scaling study: sweep, fit, extrapolate, error bars
md: A scaling study is an experiment design problem: budgets spread over orders of magnitude, sizes that bracket each valley, a properly ended schedule per run, then two fits (IsoFLOP parabolas and the parametric form) that should agree, each with bootstrap error bars.

courseTitle: Search evaluation basics: precision, recall, MAP, MRR and nDCG
lessonTitle: Graded relevance and nDCG: rewarding the best result first
md: nDCG@k answers: what fraction of the best achievable discounted gain did the top k results capture? It is the default when labels are graded and users look mostly at the first page.

courseTitle: Text embeddings and semantic search
lessonTitle: Where dense retrieval fails: hybrid search and re-ranking
md: Each stage covers another's blind spot: BM25 for rare exact terms, the bi-encoder for meaning across different words, the cross-encoder for precise final ordering on a short list. Evaluate the whole pipeline on your own queries with a metric such as recall at k (the share of relevant passages that appear in the top k results).

courseTitle: Tokenization with Byte Pair Encoding (BPE)
lessonTitle: Build a byte-level BPE tokenizer in Python
md: Decode with `errors="replace"` (or keep bytes) whenever ids can be cut at arbitrary points: one token at a time while streaming, or a sequence the model generated that may not be valid UTF-8. With strict decoding a partial character raises an error. When streaming, keep the bytes and only show the characters once all their bytes have arrived.

courseTitle: Training deep nets in practice: init, optimizers, schedules, debugging
lessonTitle: Residual connections: why 56 layers trained worse than 20
md: A residual block computes $x + F(x)$. The identity path makes doing nothing easy to learn and gives the gradient a direct route to every layer. Start each branch near zero so that a deep stack begins as one identity map rather than a variance amplifier.

courseTitle: Vector search and ANN: how HNSW finds neighbors fast
lessonTitle: Why exact nearest-neighbor search stops scaling
md: ANN indexes trade a little recall for orders of magnitude fewer distance computations. Every ANN number you read (or report) should come as a pair: recall@k and speed, measured against exact brute-force results on the same queries.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: Version ranges and lockfiles: why new code arrives unasked
md: A lockfile only protects installs that use it. A Dockerfile that copies only package.json, `npx some-tool`, a global install, or a developer running `npm update` all resolve ranges fresh. The axios post-mortem told users who were "pinned to a clean version" and ran no fresh install in the window that they were fine.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: xz-utils I: two years of patient social engineering
md: The xz attack was a trust attack, not a technical exploit of git, signing or builds. Every step was done by a legitimate maintainer with legitimate rights. Defences are partly social: fund and share maintenance of critical projects, add second reviewers for releases, and treat sudden pressure to hand over control or upgrade fast as a warning sign.

courseTitle: Synthetic data and model collapse
lessonTitle: Using synthetic data well: filter, diversify, anchor
md: Synthetic data are useful when an outside signal decides what is kept, diversity is designed in, and real data stay in the training mix. Model collapse is what happens when all three are missing.

courseTitle: System calls and mmap
lessonTitle: When a system call blocks: sleeping, short counts and EINTR
md: Every `read` and `write` may block, move fewer bytes than asked, or fail with `EINTR` or `EAGAIN`. Loop until all bytes are moved, retry on `EINTR`, and treat `EAGAIN` as "wait until the descriptor is ready".

courseTitle: System calls and mmap
lessonTitle: Watching and restricting system calls: strace, faults and seccomp
md: strace shows which calls a program makes and how often; getrusage shows the page faults that strace cannot see; seccomp turns a list of needed calls into an enforced allow-list. All three work on syscall numbers and miss the vDSO.

courseTitle: Temporal reasoning: years of experience and current roles
lessonTitle: Normalizing partial dates and Present against a reference date
md: A relative expression has no value until it is anchored. *Present*, *now*, *today*, *last year* and *the past 5 years* all need a reference date, and the normalizer should receive it as an explicit input, never read a hidden clock or let a model guess it.

courseTitle: Test-time compute scaling: sampling, search and thinking longer
lessonTitle: Coverage: how pass@k grows with the number of samples
md: Coverage is an **upper bound** on accuracy. It equals real accuracy only if you have a perfect checker (unit tests, a proof checker). For a math word problem, pass@100 = 83% means 83% of problems have *some* correct sample, not that you can find it.

courseTitle: Test-time compute scaling: sampling, search and thinking longer
lessonTitle: Thinking longer: reasoning models and budget forcing
md: Do not assume more thinking tokens never hurt. Evaluate a reasoning model at several reasoning lengths on your own tasks. Wasted tokens on easy prompts (overthinking) and how to train them away are the subject of the efficient-reasoning course, a follow-on to this one.

courseTitle: Test-time training and learned memory: TTT layers and Titans
lessonTitle: Titans: surprise, momentum and a forget gate for neural memory
md: Titans' memory update = gradient descent with momentum (carry surprise forward) and weight decay (forget), all gated per token. Momentum keeps writing after a surprising event; forgetting keeps a fixed-size memory from overflowing.

courseTitle: Thread caches and magazines
lessonTitle: Sizing M, filling the depot, and the memory you pay
md: A per-CPU or per-thread cache is a deliberate trade of memory for scalability. Idle rounds look like a leak in heap profiles and in RSS (resident set size, the physical memory a process currently holds), and they multiply by the number of CPUs (or threads) and caches. Every production design pairs its caches with a sizing policy and a way to give memory back.

courseTitle: Threat hunting
lessonTitle: From hunt to detection: the FireEye countermeasures
md: Hunts and detections are two ends of one pipeline. Precise, low-volume hunts become alerts; noisy but valuable ones become scheduled hunts with an owner and a review rhythm, like FireEye's supplemental rules. A hunt that never feeds detection leaves the organisation exactly as blind as before, once the hunter moves on.

courseTitle: Cyber threat intelligence
lessonTitle: The Diamond Model: one event, four corners
md: Two traps. First, Type 2 infrastructure is what victims usually see, so an IP address's owner is often another victim, not the adversary. Second, a shared feature is a lead, not a link: two events that share a widely used tool are not necessarily the same adversary (the attribution lesson returns to this).

courseTitle: Thinking like an attacker: threat models and security principles
lessonTitle: Assets and adversaries: what is worth taking, and by whom
md: Do not let one view take over. The Threat Modeling Manifesto lists *tendency to overfocus* as an anti-pattern: avoid exaggerating attention on adversaries, assets, or techniques. A model built only around a feared attacker misses dull, likely failures.

courseTitle: Thinking like an attacker: threat models and security principles
lessonTitle: Case: Target 2013, a vendor login across a trust boundary
md: Compliance is not security. The Senate timeline notes that Target was certified compliant with PCI DSS (Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard, the card industry's security rules) in September 2013, two months before the breach. An audit checks controls at a moment; a threat model asks how an attacker would get from here to there.

courseTitle: Time-series forecasting: baselines, smoothing and honest backtests
lessonTitle: Forecasting is supervised learning where the future is off limits
md: A random train/test split on a time series leaks the future into training and makes every model look better than it will be in production. Hyndman and Athanasopoulos state the rule plainly: the training set may contain only observations that occurred before the test observations, so no future observations are used to construct the forecast.

courseTitle: TLS and PKI in practice
lessonTitle: Downgrade attacks: POODLE, BEAST, Logjam and the fixes
md: Downgrade defence has two halves: **authenticate the negotiation** (transcript signatures, the sentinel, SCSV) and **delete the weak options** so there is nothing to downgrade to. The second is the one that always works.

courseTitle: Triton kernels: block-level GPU programming
lessonTitle: From threads to blocks: the Triton programming model
md: A Triton program instance is not one thread. It is closer to a CUDA thread block: one program becomes `num_warps` warps of 32 threads each, so with the default `num_warps=4` a single program runs on 128 threads.

courseTitle: Unified multimodal models: one transformer that reads and draws
lessonTitle: Attention masks for mixed text and image sequences
md: The rule that keeps any mask honest: a position may only attend to what will exist when it is generated. Bidirectional attention inside an image is legal exactly when the whole image is produced together, as in diffusion, flow or masked prediction. Under token-by-token generation it would leak the answer.

courseTitle: Unikernels: one application, one address space, one VM image
lessonTitle: Syscalls become function calls: one address space, one privilege level
md: Running an unmodified binary on a unikernel does not get you function-call costs. Trapping and translating each `syscall` cost 84 cycles in Unikraft's measurement, 21 times a function call. Relinking against the libOS is what removes the crossing.

courseTitle: Unikernels: one application, one address space, one VM image
lessonTitle: The spectrum: Linux-based unikernels, microVMs and sandboxes
md: Unikernel gains split into **removing the crossing** (small for real applications, per Lupine) and **specializing** (large). Linux can deliver much of the second. Choose a libOS unikernel when you also want tiny images, millisecond boots and a minimal attack surface, and can accept its limits.

courseTitle: Vector database internals: SIMD kernels, segments and disk
lessonTitle: Durability and memory tiers: WAL, mmap and disk-based ANN
md: Durability comes from the log, not the index: indexes are rebuilt or replayed from the WAL. Speed comes from what fits in RAM: keep the navigation data (graph upper layers, compressed vectors) in memory, and make every disk read count.

courseTitle: verl: the HybridFlow RL training stack for LLMs
lessonTitle: The V1 trainer: TransferQueue, sync and async modes, partial rollout
md: Async is not free. Every async mode trains on tokens from older weights, so pair it with a staleness bound and a correction mode, and watch `training/off_policy/*`. `separate_async` also needs a network checkpoint engine (`nccl`, `nixl` or `mooncake`, not `naive`) and its batch invariant, or startup fails.

courseTitle: Video world models: Genie, latent actions and neural game engines
lessonTitle: Measuring world models, and where Genie 2 and 3 go next
md: FVD alone cannot tell whether a model listens to actions. A model that ignores the controls but produces realistic clips can score well. That is why Genie pairs FVD with delta PSNR, and why its pixel-input LAM was chosen despite a slightly worse Platformers FVD (40.1 vs 38.8): its controllability was much higher (1.91 vs 1.33).

courseTitle: Fine-tuning a vision model (ViT)
lessonTitle: Linear probe, LoRA or full fine-tune: choosing what to train
md: Kumar et al. note fine-tuning can still beat linear probing out of distribution when the pretrained features are weak or the shift is small (CIFAR-10 to CIFAR-10.1, a fresh test set collected the same way as the original). LP-FT is a strong default, not a law.

courseTitle: Visual tokenizers: turning images into discrete tokens
lessonTitle: Codebook collapse: measuring and fixing unused codes
md: Bigger codebooks do not automatically mean more capacity. FSQ, a quantizer with a fixed grid of codes that lesson 5 covers (Mentzer et al., 2023), found that VQ's reconstruction FID was best at about 2^11 codes and then stopped improving, at the same point where VQ's codebook usage began to drop, despite an entropy regulariser (an extra loss that rewards spreading choices evenly over the codes).

courseTitle: vLLM attention backends: selection, batching, KV layout, CUDA graphs
lessonTitle: KV cache layout and block sizes per backend
md: A KV cache layout is chosen once for the whole model, not per layer. If two backends in one model share no layout, startup fails with *No KV cache layout satisfies every supported set* rather than converting at runtime.

courseTitle: Vision-language models for reading images
lessonTitle: Reading a receipt into validated JSON
md: Validate meaning, not just shape. Documents carry their own checksums: line items sum to a subtotal, subtotal plus tax equals the total, dates fall in a plausible range. Use them.

courseTitle: Wait-free algorithms: bounded progress for every thread
lessonTitle: Herlihy's universal construction: announce, then help
md: Universal does not mean practical. Every cell carries a full object state, and every operation contends on the single end of one log, so operations on different parts of the object (a queue's head and tail) still conflict. Kogan and Petrank point to these two costs, state copying and no disjoint-access parallelism, as why universal constructions are hardly considered practical.

courseTitle: Weather and climate foundation models: GraphCast to Aurora
lessonTitle: Uncertainty: GenCast's diffusion ensembles and CRPS
md: CRPS = accuracy minus half the spread. It rewards ensembles that are both close to the truth and honestly spread, and reduces to absolute error for one forecast.

courseTitle: Web application testing and bug bounty practice
lessonTitle: Testing sessions: tokens, cookie flags, fixation and logout
md: Four session questions: is the token random, is it protected in the browser, is it replaced at login, and does the server forget it at logout? Each has a WSTG ID and a replay you can run with your own account.

courseTitle: Web application testing and bug bounty practice
lessonTitle: Coordinated disclosure: when and how to publish
md: Publish when the rules allow, after deployers can protect themselves, with secrets and other people's data removed. The goal of disclosure is to reduce harm, not to prove you were first.

courseTitle: The browser security model
lessonTitle: HTTPS, mixed content and HSTS: keeping the network out
md: Firesheep's full fix is three layers: **HTTPS on every page** (nothing worth stealing in clear text), **`Secure` cookies** (the session never rides a plain request, even one an attacker tricks the browser into making), and **HSTS** (the browser refuses plain HTTP and certificate click-through for the whole site).

courseTitle: Windows for security: accounts, processes, registry and event logs
lessonTitle: Processes, services and svchost: what runs, and as whom
md: For every unknown process or service ask: which account (token), which file path, which parent, and when was it created? Those four facts come from Task Manager, Get-CimInstance, 4688 and 7045.

courseTitle: Wireless and mobile security
lessonTitle: WPA3: SAE, protected management frames and Enhanced Open
md: SAE moves password guessing from offline (unlimited, invisible) to online (one try per handshake, visible to the AP). PMF stops forged disconnections. OWE encrypts open networks but does not authenticate them. None of them makes a weak password strong against online guessing.

courseTitle: Wireless and mobile security
lessonTitle: Zero-click attacks: from Trident to the Pixel 9 chain
md: Zero-click attack surface is every parser that runs on attacker-supplied data before the user acts. New convenience features (previews, transcription, search) add parsers. Defence is architectural: fewer and memory-safe parsers, tight sandboxes, unreachable drivers, and short patch times.

courseTitle: WSD learning-rate schedules
lessonTitle: Why the loss plunges during the decay: the river valley picture
md: A lower LR does not remove the hill instantly: the walls only pull the iterate down while it still takes steps of reasonable size. That is why the cooldown needs a minimum length. MiniCPM found a 2.5% decay falls short where 10% suffices.

courseTitle: Zero-copy I/O: sendfile, splice and MSG_ZEROCOPY
lessonTitle: splice and tee: pipes as buffers of page references
md: Pipes are the kernel's zero-copy buffer: slots of reference-counted page pointers. splice moves those pointers between a pipe and any descriptor, tee duplicates them, and sendfile itself runs on this machinery with a hidden internal pipe.

courseTitle: Zero-shot classification: labels chosen at inference time
lessonTitle: Prompting an LLM and calibrating its label bias
md: Constrain the LLM to the label set, read a probability per label, and divide by the probabilities a content-free input gets under the same prompt. Calibration fixes a constant shift; it cannot fix a model that does not understand the labels.
